clips.title: How to study to maximize performance | Elizabeth Bjork & Robert Bjork | TEDxManhattanBeach
clips.why: Two researchers who have studied memory for decades explain why the way of studying that feels best is often the way that teaches least.
look: The difference between performance (how well you do while studying) and learning (what is still there later).
Why fast, smooth progress during study can fool you about how much you will keep.
clips.after: This is the trap in the Story of this lesson: watching every clip in order feels smooth, which is exactly why each lesson also makes you practise, build and answer.

clips.title: How to study to maximize performance | Elizabeth Bjork & Robert Bjork | TEDxManhattanBeach
clips.why: The same talk, on the two habits this course is built around: spreading study over days, and pulling things out of memory instead of reading them again.
look: Spacing: why a gap between study sessions helps, even though the second session feels harder.
Retrieval: why answering a question from memory changes what you remember, more than another reading does.
Notice that both habits feel less pleasant in the moment than cramming or rereading.
clips.after: Practice, Build and the Checkpoint are retrieval, and Come back to these in a few days is spacing: two small habits that decide whether you can do the tickets later.

clips.title: Docker in 100 Seconds
clips.why: Docker is one of the four things you prepare in this lesson; this is the fastest clear picture of what it does and why so many labs use it.
look: A container shares the host's operating system, which is why it starts in seconds where a virtual machine takes minutes.
The three words: a Dockerfile describes an image, and an image runs as a container.
clips.after: Many labs start a database, a server or a small service in a container on your laptop, so docker info must work before those labs can.

practice.q: Put the life of a checked lab in order, from the first command to a passed lab.
items: Run ./academy lab <id> from the course folder
Run the Follow along commands and compare your output with the page
Run ./academy check and read the first ✘ line
Write the missing piece, using ./academy hint when you are stuck
Run ./academy check again until every line is ✔ and it prints a pass code
Paste the pass code on the lesson page
practice.why: The lab starts by copying the starter code, and the first check shows you what is missing. You loop between writing and checking, and the pass code is the proof the lesson page accepts.

practice.q: You have read the Understand step of a lesson twice and it feels clear. What is the best next move?

options.text: Read it a third time to be sure.
options.why: Rereading makes the page feel familiar, and familiar is easy to confuse with knowing.

options.text: Close the lesson and write down the main idea and one example from memory, then compare.
options.why: Pulling the idea out of memory is retrieval, the habit from the second clip. The gaps you find are exactly what to look at again.

options.text: Move to the next lesson while it is fresh.
options.why: Moving on is fine later, but without one retrieval first you do not know what you really kept.

practice.q: You are stuck on a checked lab and want a small push, not the answer. Complete the command.
practice.hint: One word. Run it again and the next one is bigger.
practice.why: ./academy hint gives one hint at a time, from a nudge to almost the answer, and remembers how many you have seen.

practice.q: You marked six lessons done in Chrome at work. At home you open the course in Safari and the map says 0 lessons done. Why?

options.text: Progress is saved on a server and Safari has not synced yet.
options.why: There is no server. The course is a static site, and nothing about you leaves your browser.

options.text: Progress lives in each browser's local storage, so Safari at home starts from zero.
options.why: Local storage belongs to one browser on one machine. Use one browser for the course.

options.text: Marking a lesson done only lasts for one day.
options.why: It lasts until you clear the site's data. The difference here is the browser, not the time.

practice.after: or newer, git, and a running Docker.
practice.hint: Check it with node --version. The platform itself uses the version two above it.
practice.why: Node 22 or newer runs every lab. The platform runs on Node 24, which is a fine choice if you install Node today.

practice.q: A drill asks something you have not learned yet. What should you do?

options.text: Guess, commit to an answer, then read why it was right or wrong.
options.why: A guess before the explanation, even a wrong one, makes the right answer easier to remember. Wrong answers in Practice cost nothing.

options.text: Skip it and come back after reading the whole lesson.
options.why: You lose the cheapest moment to learn: the one where you have to think before you are told.

options.text: Open the Understand step in another tab and find the answer first.
options.why: That turns the drill into reading again. The point of the drill is the effort of answering.
